food.text: In 1005, the Fatimid ruler of Egypt, el-Hakem be Amr Ellah, issued a decree forbidding his subjects from eating mulukhiyah, a leafy green stew thought to be an aphrodisiac. His successor al-Zahir later allowed it again. The Druze, who hold al-Hakim in high regard, still observe the ban today.

Medieval Egypt's fertile lands, nourished by the Nile, supported both native and introduced crops. Rice, sugarcane and citrus fruits arrived following the Arab conquest in 641 CE. Egypt's central position in the Islamic world also brought Turks, Kurds and Persians, whose culinary traditions enriched local cooking.

In medieval Cairo, the making of ful was monopolized by the people living around the Princess Baths. Bath attendants heated huge pots of water there with garbage as fuel, since wood was scarce. When the baths closed, the embers kept burning, so cauldrons of fava beans simmered through the night to provide breakfast for Cairo.

The Kanz al-Fawa'id fi Tanwi' al-Mawa'id, a 14th-century Egyptian cookbook, records a recipe for mulukhiyah, glossed as a meat stew with Jew's mallow. The dish is also attested in other medieval Arabic cookbooks. Its leaves come from Corchorus olitorius, and the boiled broth is thick and mucilaginous, rather like cooked okra.

Recipes in the 14th-century cookbook Kanz al-Fawa'id reflect Egypt's diversity. Dishes from Morocco, Persia and Byzantium appear alongside local specialties. The book gives modern readers insight into the culinary practices of the era.

Soba, the capital of the Nubian kingdom of Alodia, prospered as a trading hub, with goods arriving from Makuria, the Middle East, western Africa, India and even China. Later, from 1150 to 1500, severe droughts struck Sub-Saharan Africa. Archeobotanical evidence from Soba suggests the town suffered from overgrazing and overcultivation.

Medieval sources disagree about millet in Egypt. Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi (1162-1231) said it was unknown outside a small area of Upper Egypt. Muhammad ibn Iyas (1448-1522) wrote that eating it in Cairo was unusual, but Shihab al-Umari (1301-1384) called it among the most popular cereal grains in Egypt.

Ful was prepared from the small, round bean known in Egypt as ful medames, meaning brown beans. Egyptian cooks also used other kinds, such as ful rumi, meaning European broad beans, and ful baladi, meaning country beans of middling size. The beans are cooked until very soft.

The huge pots at Cairo's Princess Baths were called qidras. Cookshops throughout Cairo sent their minions there to buy wholesale ful. The baths stood near the Mosque of Sultan al-Muayyad and the 11th-century Bab Zuweila gate.

art.text: In 1176 Saladin ordered the construction of the Cairo Citadel. It became the center of government in Egypt until the 19th century, and it was completed under sultan Al-Kamil, who ruled from 1218 to 1238.

The Mamluks, a military corps under the Ayyubid dynasty recruited from slaves, took power in 1250 and ruled Egypt until the Ottoman conquest of 1517. Their internal politics were often violent. Even so, the Mamluk sultans were generous patrons of architecture and are responsible for much of the monumental heritage of historic Cairo.

Medieval Nubia's Christian kingdoms of Makuria, Nobadia and Alodia built distinct architecture, such as the Faras Cathedral with elaborate friezes and wall paintings and the Great Monastery of St Anthony. Most of these buildings were excavated and documented before Lake Nasser's waters submerged them in the 1960s and 70s.

From around 500 CE until circa 1500 CE, Christian kingdoms thrived in Upper Nubia and southwards along the Nile. They built cities with monasteries, palaces, fortifications and cathedrals, showing influences of Coptic and Byzantine cultures from Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean.

Al-Kamil's fortifications at the Cairo Citadel can be identified by their embossed, rusticated masonry, whereas Saladin's towers have smooth dressed stones. This heavier rustic style became a common feature in other Ayyubid fortifications.

After the domination of the Shi'a Fatimids, the Ayyubid rulers were eager to promote the restoration of Sunni Islam by building Sunni madrasas. The first Sunni madrasa in Egypt was commissioned by Saladin near the Mausoleum of Imam al-Shafi'i in Cairo's Southern Cemetery.

Among the buildings of medieval Nubia was the Throne Hall of the Makurian kings in Old Dongola, described as a massive, defence-like building. Like the Faras Cathedral, it was excavated and documented before the waters of Lake Nasser submerged it.
It is recorded that the cathedral of Dongola was converted into a mosque in 1317, as the region moved from Christianity toward Islam.

Under the Baqt treaty, which was kept for six hundred years, Nubia's main exports were dates and slaves. Ivory and gold were also exchanged for Egyptian ceramics, textiles and glass, which brought Egyptian crafts into Nubia.

war.text: In 1260 the Mamluk sultan Qutuz defeated the army of Hulagu Khan at the Battle of Ain Jalut. The victory let him regain all of Syria except for the Crusader strongholds. On the way back to Egypt, Qutuz died and Baybars took the sultanate.

When Hulegu sent envoys to Cairo with a letter demanding that Qutuz surrender Egypt, Qutuz responded by killing the envoys. He then displayed their severed heads on the Bab Zuweila gate of Cairo. The battle that followed on 3 September 1260 marked the first major halt to Mongol advances.

At Montgisard on 25 November 1177, the leprosy-stricken Baldwin IV of Jerusalem, his teenage body ravaged by aggressive leprosy and his hands bandaged to cover his sores, fought in the thick of the battle and routed Saladin's Egyptian army, pursuing it for twelve miles. Saladin's men were quickly overwhelmed, and the sultan narrowly evaded capture, according to Ralph de Diceto, on the swift back of a camel. He fled back to Cairo, reaching it on 8 December with only a tenth of his army. The victory was costly: Roger de Moulins, Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller, reported that 1,100 men had been killed and 750 returned home wounded.

In 1276 the Mamluk sultan Baybars reached Dongola and defeated King David of Makuria in battle. David had attacked Aydhab and Aswan, provoking the Mamluk response. A Mamluk puppet king was then installed in Dongola.

At Ain Jalut the Mamluks used hit-and-run tactics and a feigned retreat by the general Baibars, drawing Kitbuqa's Mongols into the highlands. There Mamluk forces hidden among the trees emerged, fired arrows and attacked with cavalry, surrounding the Mongols on all sides. A final flanking maneuver by Qutuz forced the Mongol army to retreat toward Bisan, and a final Mamluk counterattack killed many Mongols, including Kitbuqa himself. Kitbuqa had led only about 10,000 troops west of the Euphrates after Hulegu withdrew most of his army.

Louis IX of France led the Seventh Crusade to Egypt, and its troops took a deserted Damietta in June 1249 after the terrified inhabitants fled. For many weeks the Muslims used guerrilla tactics against the Crusader camps, and many Crusaders were captured and sent to Cairo. The Crusaders were later besieged, and struck by disease they withdrew to Damietta on April 5, 1250, followed closely by the Muslim forces.

When the Ayyubid Sultan as-Salih Ayyub died during the Seventh Crusade, his widow Shajar al-Durr concealed the news for some time. She sent Faris ad-Din Aktai to Hasankeyf to recall Turanshah, the heir, to lead the Egyptian army.

Before Montgisard, Baldwin and Raynald of Châtillon retreated into Ascalon when they saw how massively outnumbered they were. Believing Baldwin was no threat, Saladin moved toward Jerusalem, while his army looted the kingdom as it went. Many of the able-bodied men Baldwin had summoned in his arrière-ban were captured and sold into slavery by Saladin's army. Baldwin then broke out of Ascalon along the coast with the Templars, and Saladin had sent no scouts to watch the city.

After his defeat at Dongola, King David fled south to al-Abwab. Its king, Adur, handed him over to the Muslims. According to al-Nuwayri, this happened after Adur defeated David in battle and captured him. Al-Mufaddal said Adur handed him over because he was afraid of the Mamluk Sultan.

In 1311 Kudanbes killed his brother Ayay and usurped the Makurian throne. The Mamluk sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad eventually sent an expedition to install Abdallah Barshanbu, a convert to Islam, who became Makuria's first Muslim king in 1316. Deeply unpopular, he was slain in late 1317 by another Muslim named Muhammad, a nephew of king David and Emir of the Banu Kanz tribe from Aswan.

literature.text: Ibn al-Farid, born in Cairo in 1181, was esteemed as the greatest mystic poet of the Arabs. His verse was full of Sufi imagery, and some of his poems are said to have been written in ecstasies.

Under Islam, Egypt remained a great source of literary activity, now written in Arabic. In 970 al-Azhar University was founded in Cairo, and it remains the most important center of Sunni Islamic learning. In the 12th century the Jewish Talmudic scholar Maimonides produced his most important work in Egypt.

Many tales of the One Thousand and One Nights can be traced to medieval Egyptian storytelling traditions. These stories were probably in circulation before they were collected and codified into a single collection.
Under Muslim rule, Egyptian literature changed. Libraries thrived, and the focus of writing shifted almost entirely to Islam.
Under Islam, Egypt continued to be a great source of literary endeavor, now in the Arabic language. Earlier, Egyptian monasteries had produced ascetic literature in Coptic.

Ibn al-Farid refused the patronage that other poets of his day accepted, since it would have meant writing propaganda. He preferred the humble life of a teacher, holding a position at the Al-Azhar Mosque. When the Ayyubid sultan al-Malik al-Kamil liked his odes so much that he sent a large sum of money and offered to build a shrine for him, he declined both.

By the 15th century, the Nights had absorbed three distinct layers of storytelling. Medieval Egyptian folklore was one, alongside ancient Indian and Persian folklore, and stories from Abbasid-era Baghdad.
An early novel written in Arab Egypt was Ibn al-Nafis' Theologus Autodidactus. It was a theological novel whose futuristic elements have been described as science fiction by some scholars.
In 12th-century Egypt, the Jewish Talmudic scholar Maimonides produced his most important work.
Beginning in the 14th century, Egyptian authors often placed a taqriz in their works. This was a signed statement of praise, similar to a blurb but longer.

science.text: In 1006, the Egyptian astronomer Ali ibn Ridwan observed the supernova known as SN 1006. It is regarded as the brightest stellar event in recorded history, and his account of it is the most detailed one that survives.

In the 14th century, the Egyptian scholar Najm al-Din al-Misri wrote a treatise around 1325 describing over 100 different types of scientific and astronomical instruments. He invented many of them himself.
The astronomer Ibn Yunus spent many years recording the Sun's position with a large astrolabe nearly 1.4 meters across. His work produced more than 10,000 entries. He lived from about 950 to 1009.
The astrolabic quadrant was invented in Egypt in the 11th or 12th century. It was later known in Europe as the Quadrans Vetus, meaning Old Quadrant.

Ali ibn Ridwan described the supernova of 1006 in precise terms. He said the object was two to three times as large as the disc of Venus and about one-quarter the brightness of the Moon. He also noted that the star sat low on the southern horizon.
Ibn Yunus's observations of eclipses stayed useful for centuries. They were still being used in Simon Newcomb's investigations of the motion of the Moon.

Egyptians built boats of papyrus reeds from the very beginning of their history until about 1000 CE. Around that time papyrus began to run short, which ended a co-existence with wooden watercraft that had lasted more than 4000 years.

Ibn Yunus's other observations inspired later European work as well. They were a source of inspiration for Laplace's studies of the Obliquity of the Ecliptic and the Inequalities of Jupiter and Saturn.

politics.text: Egypt's Bahri Mamluk rulers greatly enhanced the power and prestige of Egypt. Under them, Cairo grew from a small town into one of the foremost cities in the world. Baybars ruled as sultan from 1260 to 1277, and al-Ashraf Khalil captured Acre in 1291.

The Mamluk Sultanate was ruled by a military caste of mamluks, freed slave soldiers, headed by a sultan. It was established in 1250 with the overthrow of the Ayyubid dynasty in Egypt, and it lasted until the Ottoman Empire conquered it in 1517. Cairo was its capital.

Saladin founded the Sultanate of Egypt in 1171 by abolishing the Fatimid Caliphate. He had first come to Egypt leading an army against the Crusaders, where he was made vizier. His campaigns set the general borders of the sultanate for almost 350 years.

In 1260 the Mamluks under Sultan Qutuz and Baybars routed the Mongols under Kitbuqa at the Battle of Ain Jalut, halting their southward expansion. On his triumphant return to Cairo, Qutuz was assassinated in a Bahri plot, and Baybars assumed power in October 1260. Baybars also reestablished the Abbasid dynasty of caliphs in Cairo, though their role was only ceremonial.

The Ayyubid sultan Najm al-Din recaptured Jerusalem in 1244. He brought Mamluk forces into his army to hold off the crusaders, a decision he came to regret. The Ayyubids were overthrown by these bodyguards, the Mamluks.
After Saladin died in 1193, his sons contested control of the sultanate. His brother al-Adil ultimately became sultan in 1200, and all later Ayyubid sultans of Egypt were his descendants.

The Mamluk ruler invaded Nubia in 1276 after an interruption in the annual tribute of slaves, and declared himself sovereign over half of Nubia. The cathedral of Dongola had been converted to a mosque by 1317, and in the fourteenth century the Dongolan government collapsed.

The sultanate enjoyed a long period of stability and prosperity during the third reign of al-Nasir Muhammad, from 1310 to 1341. To secure it, in 1310 he imprisoned, exiled or killed any Mamluk emirs who had supported those who toppled him before, and in 1311 and 1316 he imprisoned and executed most of his father's mamluks, reducing their number to 2,000. After his death, his sons succeeded him amid internal strife, and real power was held by senior emirs.

Sultan as-Salih Ayyub died in 1249 and was succeeded in Egypt by his son al-Mu'azzam Turanshah. Turanshah alienated the Mamluk generals who had just repelled a Crusader invasion of the Nile Delta, and he constantly threatened them. Fearing for their positions, the Bahri Mamluks revolted and killed him in April 1250, which effectively ended Ayyubid power in Egypt.
In 1382 the Circassian Barkuk was proclaimed sultan, ending the Bahri dynasty. He was expelled in 1389 but recaptured Cairo in 1390. He then set up the Burji dynasty.

Joel, a 15th-century king of Makuria, is one of the last kings of Christian Nubia in the historical record. He is known from a graffito in Faras Cathedral, an inscription in the Church of Tamit, and a 1484 letter from Gebel Adda. Mamluks under Qaitbay likely conquered Dotawo before 1496.

Al-Kamil lost Damietta to the Crusaders in 1219 during the Fifth Crusade. He defeated their advance on Cairo by flooding the Nile, and they were forced to evacuate Egypt in 1221. Later, during the Sixth Crusade, he gave up cities in Palestina and Syria to Frederick II to gain his help against Damascus.
Barkuk was proclaimed sultan in 1382, ending the Bahri dynasty, after a revolt in Syria spread to Egypt in 1377. He was expelled in 1389 but recaptured Cairo in 1390, setting up the Burji dynasty.

In 1365 a civil war forced the Makurian court to flee to Gebel Adda in Lower Nubia, while Dongola was destroyed and left to the Arabs. Makuria afterwards continued only as a petty kingdom. It saw one last prosperous reign under King Joel, who is dated to 1463-1484.

Barquq died in 1399 and was succeeded by his eleven-year-old son an-Nasir Faraj. That year Timur invaded Syria, sacking Aleppo and Damascus, and his raids were devastating. A famine struck Egypt in 1403, a severe plague followed in 1405, and a Bedouin revolt practically ended Mamluk control of Upper Egypt between 1401 and 1413.

In 1310, under the patronage of the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, Hama was restored to the Ayyubids under the geographer and author Abu al-Fida. His son al-Afdal Muhammad eventually lost the favor of his Mamluk overlords and was removed in 1341, when Hama was formally placed under Mamluk rule.

philosophy.text: The Fatimid Caliphate, followers of Ismailism, a branch of Shia Islam, conquered Egypt in 969 CE. They built mosques and institutions, including Al-Azhar University, but failed to entrench Ismailism among the population. Internal sectarian conflict, combined with political instability, contributed to the reestablishment of Sunni Islam under the Ayyubid dynasty in 1171, led by Saladin.

After the Arabs took Egypt, Makuria was strong enough to halt the southern expansion of Islam. A treaty with Dongola, called Baqt, allowed peaceful coexistence and trade, and it was kept for six hundred years. Over that time Arab traders introduced Islam to Nubia, and it gradually supplanted Christianity.
The Christian kingdoms of Makuria and Alodia endured for roughly a millennium. Yet the shift in faith was visible in stone: by 1317 the cathedral of Dongola had been converted to a mosque.
Christianity did not disappear from Nubia overnight. There are records of a bishop Timothy at Qasr Ibrim in 1372, and his see included Faras.

Al-Qalqashandi wrote in 1412 that the king of al-Abwab had a similar titulature to the king of Armenia, implying that al-Abwab was a Christian state. Christian pottery continued to be produced in the region until the rise of the Funj.

In the 14th and 15th centuries, Bedouin tribes overran much of Nubia. They were Muslim, though only nominally, yet they still contributed to the Islamisation of the country by intermarrying with the Nubians.

According to Sudanese traditions, a Sufi teacher arrived in the region in the 15th century. Some claim he settled in Berber in 1445, while others say he settled near al-Mahmiya, north of Meroe, at the end of that century.

After Sultan Baybars defeated King David of Makuria in 1276 and a Mamluk puppet king was instated in Dongola, the puppet king was watched over by an Assassin from al-Abwab. This man was an Ismaeli Muslim, ordered by Baybars to keep watch over the Makurian puppet king.

culture.text: For about six hundred years, Christian Nubia and Muslim Egypt lived side by side under a treaty called the Baqt. Nubia paid an annual tribute of slaves, and the treaty guaranteed that any runaway slaves were returned to Nubia. It allowed peaceful coexistence and trade.

Nubia's main exports in the medieval period were dates and slaves, though ivory and gold were also exchanged for Egyptian ceramics, textiles, and glass. The slaves were partly a forced payment: under the Baqt treaty, Nubians had to send an annual tribute of slaves and other goods to the Islamic Governor at Aswan, and any runaway slaves had to be returned to Nubia. After an interruption in the slave tribute, the Egyptian Mamluk ruler invaded in 1276 and declared himself sovereign over half of Nubia.

The Baqt treaty is credited with delaying the spread of Islam into Nubia. The medieval Christian kingdoms of Nubia made this peace and trade agreement with the ruling Muslim power in Cairo, which held Islam back for centuries.

The Black Death struck Egypt in 1347, and the article says it brought significant destruction to the country's population, economy and political system. Its waves kept destroying Egypt until the early 16th century. Plague epidemics spread across the region in 1388-1389, 1397-1398 and 1403-1407, and kept returning through 1513-1514. Famine, disease, military tensions and high taxation helped bring the Mamluk period to its end.

Bedouin tribes overran most of Sudan in the 14th and 15th centuries, migrating to the Butana, the Gezira, Kordofan and Darfur. Arab tribes intermarried with Nubian and other African populations and gradually introduced Islam. This slowly reshaped the region's religion and identity.

Arab traders arriving in Nubia gradually introduced Islam, which slowly supplanted Christianity. By 1317 the cathedral of Dongola had been converted into a mosque. Yet a bishop named Timothy is still recorded at Qasr Ibrim in 1372.
